newsitem.title: USA: Senators urge tough action by NRC on safety issues.
newsitem.headline: Senators urge tough action by NRC on safety issues.

text.p: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission must slap sanctions on U.S. nuclear power plants that fail to fix problems within a reasonable time and revamp the agency's early warning system of problem plants, according to a government watchdog report issued Tuesday.

"The NRC is not doing its job," said Senator Joseph Biden (D-Del). "There is an attitude within the NRC, a culture of tolerating problems, that has allowed nuclear plants to deteriorate year after year."
Biden and Senator Joe Lieberman (D-Connn) asked the government's General Accounting Office to analyze how well the NRC oversees safety conditions at U.S. nuclear power plants.
The GAO report, released at a news briefing held by the two senators, found the NRC did not take aggressive enforcement action to force plants to fix problems.
The agency also failed to evaluate the competence of nuclear plant managers as part of the inspection process and often acted too late to identify plants with problems, the report said.
The NRC has been criticized in the past for its so-called watch list, which was often slow to identify plants with safety problems.

In January, the NRC added five nuclear power stations to the watch list including the Salem 1 unit owned by Public Service Electric and Gas, which was described by consumer group Public Citizen as the worst nuclear reactor in the nation. The agency also add the Maine Yankee plant, owned by Northeast Utilities to the list.
A total of 14 plants are now on the watch list, out of the nation's 110 nuclear plants.

"The list is not working because plants have been placed on the list too late to achieve the objective of an early warning," Lieberman said. "Others have stayed on the watch list much long, as long as seven years. By that time, their problems should be fixed or the plants closed down."
The NRC must stop giving plants years to fix problems, and instead issue sanctions to force speedy compliance, the two senators said.

The NRC should also guard against U.S. nuclear plants looking for ways to cut corners as they come under increased economic pressure from the deregulated electricity and power industry, Lieberman said.
"There is clear and evident pressure on Northeast Utilities to reopen one of its plants," Lieberman said, adding that he expected the Millstone 3 unit in Connecticut to be reopened by year-end.
Despite the critical findings, the senators expressed support for NRC Commissioner Shirley Jackson, who took over the agency in mid-1995 after teaching physics at Rutgers University.
"She is tough, she keeps her word and she is committed," Biden said. "There does seem to be a new attitude at the NRC."
Three other commissioners have been replaced at the NRC during the past two years.
The NRC said it agreed with the "basic thrust" of the issues raised in the report, and said it already had programs underway to address the problems.
"The chairman has been very aggressive in working with the staff in adopting a host of initiatives to improve the effectiveness of our agency," an NRC spokesman said.
The Senate Environment Committee's panel on nuclear regulation plans to hold a hearing on safety issues later this year, the senators said.
The nuclear industry has maintained that most plants are meeting safety standards and that the number of "significant safety events" per U.S. plant fell from 2.4 in 1985 to 0.1 in 1995.
((Washington energy desk 202 898 8467))
